paragraphs: The objection to the plan of the Convention that has had the most success in this State, and perhaps in several of the other States, is that the Constitution makes no provision for trial by jury in civil cases. The dishonest way in which this objection is usually stated has been pointed out and exposed more than once, but the opponents of the plan keep pressing it in all their conversations and writings. The mere silence of the Constitution about civil cases is presented as an abolition of trial by jury. The speeches for which this silence has served as a pretext are cleverly designed to persuade people that the supposed abolition is complete and universal, reaching not only every kind of civil case but even criminal cases. To argue about the criminal cases, however, would be as vain and fruitless as to attempt a serious proof that matter exists, or to demonstrate any of those propositions that carry conviction by their own evidence once they are put in language that conveys their meaning.

With regard to civil cases, subtleties almost too contemptible to refute have been used to support the notion that a thing which is merely not provided for has been entirely abolished. Every discerning person must see at once the wide difference between silence and abolition. But the inventors of this fallacy have tried to support it with certain legal maxims of interpretation, which they have twisted away from their true meaning, so it may not be wholly useless to examine the ground they have taken.

The maxims they rely on are of this kind: "A specification of particulars is an exclusion of generals"; or, "The expression of one thing is the exclusion of another." From these, they say, it follows that because the Constitution has established trial by jury in criminal cases and is silent about civil cases, this silence is an implied prohibition of trial by jury in the latter.

The rules of legal interpretation are rules of common sense, adopted by the courts in construing the laws. The true test of whether they are applied justly, therefore, is whether the application conforms to the source from which they come. This being so, let me ask whether it is consistent with common sense to suppose that a provision obliging the legislative power to commit the trial of criminal cases to juries takes away its right to authorize or permit that mode of trial in other cases. Is it natural to suppose that a command to do one thing is a prohibition against doing another, which the legislature already had the power to do and which is not incompatible with the thing commanded? If such a supposition would be unnatural and unreasonable, it cannot be rational to maintain that a requirement of trial by jury in certain cases forbids it in others.

A power to establish courts is a power to prescribe the mode of trial. Consequently, if the Constitution had said nothing on the subject of juries, the legislature would be free either to adopt that institution or to leave it alone. In criminal cases this discretion is limited by the express requirement of trial by jury in all such cases; but in civil cases, of course, it is left unrestricted, since there is total silence on that point. Specifying an obligation to try all criminal cases in a particular mode does exclude any obligation or necessity of using the same mode in civil cases, but it does not limit the legislature's power to use that mode if it thinks proper. The pretense, therefore, that the national legislature would not be at full liberty to submit all the civil cases of federal cognizance to the decision of juries is a pretense with no just foundation.

We have now seen that the maxims cannot support the use made of them. Let us try to establish what their proper use and true meaning are. Examples will do this best. The plan of the Convention states that the power of Congress, in other words of the national legislature, is to reach certain listed cases. Listing particulars in this way plainly rules out any claim to a general legislative authority, since it would be absurd and pointless to grant special powers affirmatively if a general authority was intended.

In the same way, the Constitution declares that the judicial authority of the federal courts comprehends certain particularly specified cases. The listing of those cases marks the precise limits beyond which the federal courts cannot extend their jurisdiction. Since the objects of their cognizance are enumerated, the specification would be meaningless if it did not exclude any idea of a more extensive authority.

These examples are enough to explain the maxims that have been mentioned and to show the way in which they should be used. But so that there may be no misunderstanding on this subject, I shall add one more case, to demonstrate the proper use of these maxims and the abuse that has been made of them.

Let us suppose that under the laws of this State a married woman was incapable of conveying her estate, and that the legislature, considering this an evil, should enact that she might dispose of her property by a deed executed in the presence of a public official. In such a case there can be no doubt that the specification would amount to an exclusion of any other mode of conveyance, because the woman had no previous power to transfer her property, and the specification determines the particular mode she is to use for that purpose. But let us further suppose that in a later part of the same act it should be declared that no woman may dispose of any estate of a given value without the consent of three of her nearest relations, shown by their signing the deed. Could anyone infer from this regulation that a married woman might not obtain her relations' approval of a deed conveying property of lesser value? The position is too absurd to merit a refutation, and yet this is precisely the position that must be established by those who contend that trial by jury in civil cases is abolished because it is expressly provided for in criminal cases.

The friends and the adversaries of the plan of the Convention, if they agree in nothing else, at least agree in the value they set upon trial by jury. If there is any difference between them, it is this: the former regard it as a valuable safeguard of liberty, while the latter call it the very palladium of free government. For my own part, the more I have seen of how the institution operates, the more reason I have found to hold it in high esteem. It would be altogether superfluous to examine how far it deserves to be thought useful or essential in a representative republic, or how much more merit it may have as a defense against the oppressions of a hereditary monarch than as a barrier against the tyranny of popular public officials in a popular government. Discussions of this kind would be more curious than beneficial, since everyone is satisfied of the usefulness of the institution and of its friendly aspect toward liberty. But I must acknowledge that I cannot readily see the inseparable connection between the existence of liberty and trial by jury in civil cases. Arbitrary impeachments, arbitrary methods of prosecuting pretended offenses, and arbitrary punishments following arbitrary convictions have always appeared to me the great engines of judicial despotism, and these all relate to criminal proceedings. Trial by jury in criminal cases, aided by the habeas corpus act, therefore seems to be the only thing concerned in the question. And both of these are provided for, in the most ample manner, in the plan of the Convention.
Some have said that trial by jury protects against oppressive use of the power of taxation. This claim deserves a closer look.

Plainly, trial by jury cannot affect the legislature's decisions about how much tax to lay, what to tax, or by what rule to apportion it. If it can have any effect at all, therefore, the effect must be on how taxes are collected and on how the officers charged with enforcing the revenue laws behave.

As for the manner of collection in this State under our own Constitution, trial by jury is in most cases not used. Taxes are usually raised by the quicker procedure of seizing and selling property, as is done for rent. Everyone acknowledges that this is essential if the revenue laws are to be effective. A slow lawsuit to recover the taxes owed by each individual would suit neither the needs of the public nor the convenience of the citizens. It would often pile up costs heavier than the tax originally due.

And as for the behavior of the revenue officers, the provision for trial by jury in criminal cases will give the security that is wanted. Deliberate abuses of public authority that oppress the subject, and every form of extortion by officials, are offenses against the government. Those who commit them may be indicted and punished as the circumstances of the case require.

The excellence of trial by jury in civil cases appears to depend on circumstances unrelated to the preservation of liberty. The strongest argument in its favor is that it is a security against corruption. There is always more time and better opportunity to tamper with a standing body of judges than with a jury summoned for the occasion, so there is reason to suppose that a corrupt influence would find its way more easily to the former than to the latter. The force of this consideration is, however, reduced by others. The sheriff, who summons ordinary juries, and the clerks of the courts, who nominate special juries, are themselves standing officers, and, acting individually, may be supposed more open to the touch of corruption than the judges, who are a collective body. It is not difficult to see that those officers would have the power to select jurors who would serve the purpose of the party as well as a corrupted bench. In the next place, it may fairly be supposed that there would be less difficulty in gaining over some of the jurors taken at random from the public at large than in gaining over men chosen by the government for their integrity and good character. But even after making every deduction for these considerations, trial by jury must still be a valuable check upon corruption. It greatly multiplies the obstacles to its success. As matters now stand, it would be necessary to corrupt both court and jury; for where the jury have gone clearly wrong, the court will generally grant a new trial, and it would in most cases be of little use to work on the jury unless the court could be gained as well. Here then is a double security, and it will readily be seen that this combined arrangement tends to preserve the purity of both institutions. By increasing the obstacles to success, it discourages attempts to seduce the integrity of either. The temptations to prostitute themselves that the judges might have to resist must certainly be much fewer, while the cooperation of a jury is necessary, than they would be if the judges had the exclusive determination of all cases.

Notwithstanding the doubts I have expressed as to whether trial by jury in civil cases is essential to liberty, therefore, I admit that in most cases, under proper regulations, it is an excellent method of deciding questions of property. On that account alone it would deserve a constitutional provision in its favor, if it were possible to fix the limits within which it ought to be confined. There is, however, great difficulty in this in all cases; and men not blinded by enthusiasm must be aware that in a federal government, which is a composition of societies whose ideas and institutions on the matter differ materially from one another, that difficulty must be not a little increased. For my own part, every time I look at the subject anew, I become more convinced of the reality of the obstacles which, we are authoritatively informed, prevented the insertion of a provision on this head in the plan of the Convention.

Few people understand how greatly the limits of jury trial differ from State to State. Because this bears considerably on the judgment we should pass on the omission complained of, I need to explain it. Of all the States, ours has judicial establishments that most closely resemble those of Great Britain. We have courts of common law, courts of probates (analogous in certain matters to the spiritual courts in England), a court of admiralty and a court of chancery. In the courts of common law only does trial by jury prevail, and even there with some exceptions. In all the others a single judge presides and proceeds in general according to the course of the canon or civil law, without the aid of a jury.(1) In New Jersey there is a court of chancery which proceeds like ours, but there are neither courts of admiralty nor of probates in the sense in which these last are established with us. In that State the courts of common law have cognizance of those cases which with us are decided in the courts of admiralty and of probates, and of course jury trial is more extensive in New Jersey than in New York. In Pennsylvania this is perhaps still more the case, for there is no court of chancery in that State, and its common-law courts have equity jurisdiction. It has a court of admiralty, but none of probates, at least on the plan of ours. Delaware has in these respects imitated Pennsylvania. Maryland comes closer to New York, as does Virginia, except that the latter has more than one chancellor. North Carolina has most in common with Pennsylvania, South Carolina with Virginia. I believe, however, that in some of those States which have separate courts of admiralty, the cases pending in them are tried by juries. In Georgia there are none but common-law courts, and an appeal of course lies from the verdict of one jury to another, which is called a special jury, and for which a particular mode of appointment is set out. In Connecticut they have no separate courts of either chancery or admiralty, and their courts of probates have no jurisdiction over cases. Their common-law courts have admiralty jurisdiction and, to a certain extent, equity jurisdiction. In cases of importance their General Assembly is the only court of chancery. In Connecticut, therefore, trial by jury extends in practice further than in any other State yet mentioned. Rhode Island is, I believe, in this respect much in the situation of Connecticut. Massachusetts and New Hampshire are in a similar position as regards the blending of law, equity and admiralty jurisdictions. In the four Eastern States trial by jury not only stands on a broader foundation than in the other States, but is attended with a peculiarity unknown, in its full extent, to any of them. There is an appeal of course from one jury to another, until there have been two verdicts out of three on one side.

From this sketch it appears that there is a material diversity, in the form as well as in the extent of the institution of trial by jury in civil cases, among the individual States. Two obvious reflections follow from this fact. First, the Convention could not have fixed upon any general rule that would have suited the circumstances of all the States. Second, more, or at least as much, might have been risked by taking the system of any one State as a standard than by omitting a provision altogether and leaving the matter, as has been done, to legislative regulation.

The proposals made to fill the gap have illustrated the difficulty more than they have removed it. The minority of Pennsylvania has proposed these words for the purpose—"Trial by jury shall be as heretofore"—and this, I maintain, would be senseless and meaningless. The United States, in their united or collective capacity, are the OBJECT to which all general provisions in the Constitution must necessarily be taken to refer. Now it is evident that although trial by jury, with various limitations, is known in each State individually, in the United States as such it is at this time altogether unknown, because the present federal government has no judiciary power whatever; and consequently there is no proper antecedent or previous establishment to which the word heretofore could relate. It would therefore lack a precise meaning and, from its uncertainty, would have no effect.

Just as the form of the provision would not fulfill the intent of its proposers, so, if I understand that intent rightly, the provision would on the other hand be inexpedient in itself. I presume the intent to be that cases in the federal courts should be tried by jury if, in the State where the court sat, that mode of trial would be used in a similar case in the State courts; that is to say, admiralty cases would be tried by a jury in Connecticut and without one in New York. The capricious operation of so dissimilar a method of trial in the same cases, under the same government, is by itself enough to turn every well-regulated judgment against it. Whether a case should be tried with or without a jury would depend, in a great number of cases, on the accidental location of the court and the parties.

But in my judgment this is not the greatest objection. I am deeply and deliberately convinced that there are many cases for which trial by jury is unsuitable. I think this especially true of cases that affect the public peace with foreign nations—that is, most cases in which the question turns wholly on the laws of nations. Among others, all prize cases are of this kind. Juries cannot be supposed competent to inquiries that demand a thorough knowledge of the laws and usages of nations. They will also sometimes be swayed by impressions that keep them from giving enough weight to the considerations of public policy that ought to guide their inquiries. There would therefore always be a danger that their decisions would violate the rights of other nations and so give occasion for reprisals and war. It is true that the proper province of juries is to decide matters of fact, but in most cases the legal consequences are so tangled up with the facts that the two cannot be separated.

It will add great weight to this remark about prize cases to mention that the method of deciding them has been thought worthy of particular regulation in various treaties between different powers of Europe, and that, under such treaties, they are decided in Great Britain, in the last resort, before the king himself in his privy council, where the facts as well as the law are re-examined. This alone demonstrates the unwisdom of inserting in the Constitution a fundamental provision that would make the State systems a standard for the national government in the article under consideration. It also shows the danger of burdening the government with any constitutional provisions whose propriety is not beyond dispute.

My convictions are equally strong that great advantages result from separating the equity jurisdiction from the law jurisdiction, and that the cases belonging to the former would be improperly committed to juries. The great and primary use of a court of equity is to give relief in extraordinary cases, which are exceptions(2) to general rules. To unite the jurisdiction over such cases with the ordinary jurisdiction must tend to unsettle the general rules and to subject every case that arises to a special determination. Separating the one from the other has the opposite effect: it makes one a sentinel over the other and keeps each within its proper limits. Besides this, the circumstances that make cases proper for courts of equity are in many instances so delicate and intricate that they are incompatible with the character of trials by jury. They often require such long, deliberate and critical investigation as would be impracticable for men called from their occupations and obliged to decide before they were permitted to return to them. The simplicity and speed that distinguish this mode of trial require that the matter to be decided be reduced to some single and obvious point, while the litigation usual in chancery frequently comprehends a long train of minute and independent particulars.

It is true that separating the equity jurisdiction from the legal jurisdiction is peculiar to the English system of jurisprudence, which several of the States have taken as their model. But it is equally true that wherever the two have been united, trial by jury has been unknown. And the separation is essential if that institution is to be kept in its original purity. A court of equity can readily extend its jurisdiction to matters of law. But there is considerable reason to suspect that extending the jurisdiction of the courts of law to matters of equity would not only fail to bring the advantages that courts of chancery can give on the plan on which they are established in this State. It would also tend, little by little, to change the nature of the courts of law and to undermine trial by jury, by bringing in questions too complicated to be decided in that mode.

These appear to be conclusive reasons against building the systems of all the States into the national judiciary, which is what the Pennsylvania minority may be guessed to have been attempting. Let us now examine how far the Massachusetts proposal is likely to cure the supposed defect.

It is in this form: "In civil actions between citizens of different States, every issue of fact, arising in actions at common law, may be tried by a jury if the parties, or either of them, request it."

This, at best, is a proposal confined to one kind of case. The fair inference is either that the Massachusetts convention considered this the only class of federal cases in which trial by jury would be proper, or that, if it desired a more extensive provision, it found it impracticable to devise one that would properly serve the purpose. If the first, the omission of a regulation concerning so limited an object can never be considered a material imperfection in the system. If the last, it strongly confirms the extreme difficulty of the thing.

But this is not all. If we recall the observations already made about the courts that exist in the individual States of the Union and the different powers exercised by them, it will appear that no expressions are more vague and indeterminate than those used to describe the kind of cases that are meant to be entitled to trial by jury. In this State the boundaries between actions at common law and actions of equitable jurisdiction are fixed in accordance with the rules that prevail in England on that subject. In many of the other States the boundaries are less precise. In some of them every case is to be tried in a court of common law, and on that footing every action may be considered an action at common law, to be decided by a jury if the parties, or either of them, choose it. Hence the same irregularity and confusion that I have already noticed as resulting from the regulation proposed by the Pennsylvania minority would be introduced by complying with this proposal. In one State a case would be decided by a jury if the parties, or either of them, requested it; but in another State a case exactly similar to the first must be decided without a jury, because the State courts differed as to common-law jurisdiction.

Clearly, then, the Massachusetts proposal cannot work as a general rule until the different States adopt some uniform plan for the limits between common-law and equitable jurisdictions. Devising such a plan is hard in itself and would take much time and thought to perfect. It would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to suggest any general regulation that all the States in the Union would accept, or that would fit exactly with the institutions of every individual State.

It may be asked, why could not a reference have been made to the constitution of this State, taking that, which I allow to be a good one, as a standard for the United States? I answer that it is not very probable that the other States would think of our institutions as we do ourselves. It is natural to suppose that they are so far more attached to their own, and that each would struggle for the preference. If the plan of taking one State as a model for the whole had been thought of in the Convention, it is to be presumed that adopting it in that body would have been made difficult by each delegation's preference for its own government; and it must be uncertain which of the States would have been taken as the model. It has been shown that many of them would be improper ones. And I leave it to conjecture whether, all things considered, it is most likely that New York or some other State would have been preferred. But suppose that a judicious selection could have been made in the Convention. There would still have been great danger of jealousy and disgust in the other States at the bias shown toward the institutions of one. The enemies of the plan would have been furnished with a fine pretext for raising a host of local prejudices against it, which might perhaps have endangered, in no small degree, its final establishment.

To avoid the difficulties of defining the cases that trial by jury ought to embrace, men of enthusiastic temper sometimes suggest that a provision might have been inserted establishing it in all cases whatsoever. For this, I believe, no precedent is to be found in any member of the Union; and the considerations that have been stated in discussing the proposal of the minority of Pennsylvania must satisfy every sober mind that establishing trial by jury in all cases would have been an unpardonable error in the plan.

In short, the more the matter is considered, the more difficult will appear the task of shaping a provision in such a form that it does not say too little to serve the purpose or too much to be advisable, and that it does not open other sources of opposition to the great and essential object of introducing a firm national government.

On the other hand, I cannot help believing that the different lights in which the subject has been placed in these observations will go far toward removing the apprehensions that open-minded persons may have felt about it. They have tended to show that the security of liberty is materially at stake only in trial by jury in criminal cases, which the plan of the Convention provides for in the most ample manner. They have also tended to show that, in by far the greatest proportion of civil cases, and in those that concern the great body of the community, that mode of trial will stay in full force as established by the State constitutions, untouched and unaffected by the plan of the Convention. They have further tended to show that the plan abolishes it(3) in no case, and that there are great, if not insurmountable, difficulties in the way of making any precise and proper provision for it in a Constitution for the United States.

The best judges of the matter will be the least anxious to have trial by jury in civil cases established in the Constitution. They will be the most ready to admit that the constant changes in the affairs of society may make a different way of deciding questions of property preferable in many of the cases where trial by jury now prevails. For my part, I acknowledge that I am convinced that even in this State it could usefully be extended to some cases to which it does not now apply, and could just as usefully be restricted in others. All reasonable men concede that it ought not to apply in all cases. Innovations that narrow its ancient limits, in these States as well as in Great Britain, strongly suggest that its former extent has been found inconvenient, and leave room to suppose that future experience may show the wisdom and usefulness of other exceptions. I suspect that, by the nature of the thing, it is impossible to fix the beneficial point at which the institution ought to stop operating, and to me this is a strong argument for leaving the matter to the discretion of the legislature.

This is now clearly understood to be the case in Great Britain, and it is equally so in the State of Connecticut. Yet it can safely be affirmed that more encroachments on trial by jury have been made in this State since the Revolution, although a positive article of our constitution provides for it, than in the same time in either Connecticut or Great Britain. It may be added that these encroachments have generally begun with the men who try to persuade the people that they are the warmest defenders of popular liberty, but who have seldom allowed constitutional obstacles to stop them in a favorite course. The truth is that the general CHARACTER of a government is all that can be substantially relied upon for lasting effects. Particular provisions, though not altogether useless, have far less virtue and effectiveness than are commonly ascribed to them; and the want of them will never be, with men of sound discernment, a decisive objection to any plan that shows the leading characters of a good government.

It certainly sounds more than a little harsh and extraordinary to claim that a Constitution offers no security for liberty, though it expressly establishes trial by jury in criminal cases, merely because it does not do so in civil cases too. Meanwhile it is notorious that Connecticut, always regarded as the most popular State in the Union, can boast of no constitutional provision for either.

1. It has been wrongly suggested that the court of chancery generally tries disputed facts by a jury. The truth is that such references to a jury seldom occur in that court, and in no case are they necessary except where the validity of a devise of land is in question.

2. It is true that the principles governing that relief have now been reduced to a regular system; but it is no less true that they apply, in the main, to SPECIAL circumstances, which form exceptions to general rules.
3. See No. 81, in which the supposition that it is abolished by vesting the appellate jurisdiction in matters of fact in the Supreme Court is examined and refuted.
